title: Mixed set 2: all units at exam pace
author: p1-mixed-author
directions: This original Liminal mixed set draws 15 multiple-choice questions from all eight units of the course at the exam's pace: 30 minutes, with a four-function, scientific or graphing calculator allowed. The questions are mixed on purpose, so part of each one is choosing the method: momentum or energy, force or torque, kinematics or a conservation law. Expect it to feel slower than practising one unit at a time. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and neglect air resistance unless a question says otherwise. Liminal's formula reference is appended; before the real exam, also practice with College Board's own equation sheet. Record raw points; they are practice evidence, not AP® scores.

figures.alt: Velocity–time graph with v in m/s from −3 to 5 and t in s from 0 to 8. Straight segments join the points (0, 4), (2, 0), (4, −2) and (8, −2).

parts.directions: Choose the best answer for each of the 15 questions and mark it on the answer sheet. Each question is worth 1 point, and there is no penalty for a wrong answer, so answer every question.

items.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up from ground level at 15 m/s. Taking up as positive and neglecting air resistance, at what time after launch is the ball 8.0 m above the ground on its way down?
items.rationale: With constant acceleration −9.8 m/s^2, y = 15t − 4.9t^2. Setting y = 8.0 m gives 4.9t^2 − 15t + 8.0 = 0, with roots t = 0.69 s (rising) and t = 2.4 s (falling). The question asks for the way down, so t ≈ 2.4 s. Energy would give the speed at 8.0 m (8.3 m/s) but not the time.

distractorNotes.A: Divides 8.0 m by 15 m/s, as if the ball kept its launch speed. It slows by 9.8 m/s every second on the way up.
distractorNotes.B: This is the earlier root, when the ball passes 8.0 m on its way up.
distractorNotes.C: This is the time to reach the top, (15 m/s)/(9.8 m/s^2). The ball then needs about another 0.84 s to fall back to 8.0 m.

items.prompt: The graph shows the velocity of a robot vacuum cleaner moving along a straight hallway, with the direction it first moves taken as positive. At what time after t = 0 is the robot back at its starting position?
items.rationale: The robot is back at its start when its displacement, the signed area between the v–t graph and the time axis, returns to zero. From 0 to 2.0 s the area is (1/2)(2.0)(4.0) = +4.0 m. From 2.0 to 4.0 s it is (1/2)(2.0)(−2.0) = −2.0 m, and after 4.0 s it changes by −2.0 m each second. The total is 4.0 − 2.0 − 2.0 = 0 at t = 5.0 s.

distractorNotes.A: At 2.0 s the velocity is zero: the robot turns around there, at its farthest point from the start.
distractorNotes.B: Treats the region from 2.0 s to 4.0 s as a rectangle of area −4.0 m. It is a triangle, of area −2.0 m.
distractorNotes.D: Leaves out the area from 2.0 s to 4.0 s and cancels the +4.0 m with the constant −2.0 m/s section alone.

items.prompt: After a brief push, a crate slides down a straight loading ramp inclined at 22° above the horizontal and moves at constant velocity. What is the coefficient of kinetic friction between the crate and the ramp?
items.rationale: Constant velocity means zero net force (Newton's first law), so along the ramp kinetic friction balances the component of gravity: μ_k mg cos 22° = mg sin 22°. So μ_k = tan 22° ≈ 0.40, whatever the crate's mass.

distractorNotes.A: Reads constant velocity as meaning no forces act along the ramp. The net force is zero, but that takes friction to balance the downhill component of gravity.
distractorNotes.C: This is cos 22°, the ratio of the normal force to the weight, not the ratio of the friction force to the normal force.
distractorNotes.D: Inverts the ratio, cos 22°/sin 22°. Friction balances mg sin 22° and the normal force is mg cos 22°, so μ_k = sin 22°/cos 22°.

items.prompt: A 1200 kg car starts from rest on a straight, level road. The road pushes forward on its drive wheels with a constant 3600 N force, and air resistance and rolling resistance together exert a constant 1200 N backward on it. Taking the car's direction of motion as positive, how far does the car travel in the first 4.0 s?
items.rationale: Newton's second law gives the acceleration from the net force and the mass: a = (3600 − 1200)/1200 = 2.0 m/s^2, constant because both forces are constant. A time is given and a distance asked for, so constant-acceleration kinematics finishes it: from rest, x = (1/2)at^2 = (1/2)(2.0)(4.0)^2 = 16 m. The vertical forces, gravity and the normal force, cancel and do not enter.

distractorNotes.A: Divides the net force by the car's weight, (1200)(9.8) = 11,760 N, instead of its mass, giving a = 0.20 m/s^2. In F_net = ma the m is the mass in kilograms.
distractorNotes.C: Uses the 3600 N forward force alone, a = 3.0 m/s^2. The acceleration comes from the net force, so the 1200 N of resistance must be subtracted.
distractorNotes.D: Writes x = at^2, leaving out the 1/2. From rest with constant acceleration, x = (1/2)at^2.

items.prompt: A rope lifts a 5.0 kg bucket of water straight up from rest with a constant tension of 70 N. What is the bucket's speed after it has risen 2.0 m?
items.rationale: By the work–energy theorem, the net work equals the change in kinetic energy. The rope does +140 J and gravity does −(5.0)(9.8)(2.0) = −98 J, so W_net = 42 J = (1/2)(5.0)v^2 and v = √16.8 ≈ 4.1 m/s. (Equivalently, a = (70 − 49)/5.0 = 4.2 m/s^2 and v^2 = 2a(2.0 m).)

distractorNotes.A: Sets the net work equal to mv^2, leaving out the 1/2.
distractorNotes.C: This is the speed after a free fall of 2.0 m, from mgh = (1/2)mv^2. The bucket rises: the rope supplies energy and gravity takes some of it away.
distractorNotes.D: Counts only the rope's work. Gravity does −98 J on the rising bucket, and the change in kinetic energy equals the work done by all the forces.

items.prompt: In which case does the named force do nonzero work on the object?
choices: The tension in a pendulum's string, on the swinging bob
Earth's gravitational force, on a satellite in a circular orbit
The normal force from a fixed ramp, on a block sliding down it
The normal force from an elevator's floor, on a passenger riding up
items.rationale: A force does work only when the displacement of its point of application has a component along the force. The elevator floor pushes the passenger upward while the passenger moves upward, so the normal force does positive work, W = F_N d. In each of the other cases the force stays perpendicular to the object's velocity.

distractorNotes.A: The tension points along the string, toward the pivot, while the bob moves along the arc, perpendicular to the string, so the tension does no work.
distractorNotes.B: In a circular orbit, gravity points toward the planet's center, perpendicular to the satellite's velocity, so it does no work and the speed stays constant.
distractorNotes.C: The normal force from a fixed ramp is perpendicular to the ramp's surface, along which the block moves, so it does no work.

items.prompt: On a level ice rink, a 0.16 kg puck moving at 9.0 m/s strikes a 0.48 kg puck at rest head-on. Just afterward, the 0.16 kg puck moves at 1.5 m/s in its original direction. The 0.48 kg puck then slides 8.0 m in a straight line before stopping. Treating the collision as brief, what is the coefficient of kinetic friction between the 0.48 kg puck and the ice?
items.rationale: During the brief collision momentum is conserved: (0.16)(9.0) = (0.16)(1.5) + (0.48)v_B, so v_B = 2.5 m/s. Kinetic energy is not conserved (6.48 J before, 1.68 J after). After the collision, the work done by friction removes the puck's kinetic energy: μ_k mgd = (1/2)mv_B^2, so μ_k = v_B^2/(2gd) = 6.25/(2(9.8)(8.0)) ≈ 0.040.

distractorNotes.B: Assumes the 0.16 kg puck stops, so that all its momentum passes to the other puck (v_B = 3.0 m/s). It keeps moving at 1.5 m/s.
distractorNotes.C: Leaves out the 1/2 in kinetic energy, μ_k = v_B^2/(gd).
distractorNotes.D: Conserves kinetic energy instead of momentum, using the 0.16 kg puck's given 1.5 m/s afterward: (1/2)(0.16)(9.0^2 − 1.5^2) = (1/2)(0.48)v_B^2 gives v_B = 5.1 m/s. A collision conserves momentum; it conserves kinetic energy only when it is elastic, and the given speeds show this one is not.

items.prompt: Sand falls straight down onto a horizontal conveyor belt at a steady 15 kg/s, and the belt carries it away at a constant 2.0 m/s. Ignoring friction in the belt's rollers, what extra horizontal force must the motor exert on the belt to keep its speed constant?
items.rationale: Each second, 15 kg of sand goes from zero horizontal velocity to 2.0 m/s, so the belt must give the sand horizontal momentum at the rate Δp/Δt = (15 kg/s)(2.0 m/s) = 30 N. By Newton's third law the sand pushes back on the belt with 30 N, which the motor must balance.

distractorNotes.A: Reasons that a belt moving at constant speed needs no net force. The belt's speed is constant, but the sand's is not: the sand must be accelerated, and its reaction acts on the belt.
distractorNotes.B: Equates the motor's power Fv to the rate at which the sand gains kinetic energy, (1/2)(15 kg/s)(2.0 m/s)^2 = 30 W. While the sand slips on the belt before matching its speed, kinetic friction converts another 30 W to internal energy, so the motor supplies 60 W and the force is 30 N.
distractorNotes.D: Uses the weight of the sand that lands each second, (15)(9.8). That force is vertical and is supported by the rollers; the horizontal force comes from the change in the sand's horizontal momentum.

items.prompt: A robotic arm turns about a fixed joint, and its gripper is 0.50 m from the joint's axis. At one instant the arm's angular speed is 2.0 rad/s and it is speeding up with an angular acceleration of 3.0 rad/s^2. What is the magnitude of the gripper's acceleration at that instant?
items.rationale: The gripper's acceleration has two perpendicular components. The tangential component, from the change in angular speed, is a_t = rα = (0.50)(3.0) = 1.5 m/s^2. The centripetal component, from the change in direction, is a_c = rω^2 = (0.50)(2.0)^2 = 2.0 m/s^2, toward the axis. They combine as √(1.5^2 + 2.0^2) = 2.5 m/s^2.

distractorNotes.A: This is only the tangential component, rα. The gripper also changes direction, which needs a centripetal component rω^2.
distractorNotes.B: This is only the centripetal component, rω^2. The arm is speeding up, so there is also a tangential component rα.
distractorNotes.D: Adds the two components as numbers. They are perpendicular, so they add as vectors.

items.prompt: A 30 kg flagpole 4.0 m long lies on level ground. It is thicker at its base, so its center of mass is 1.6 m from the base end. A worker lifts the thin top end slightly off the ground with a vertical force while the base end stays on the ground. What is the magnitude of the worker's force?
items.rationale: Take torques about the base end, which stays on the ground, so the ground's unknown force there has no torque: F(4.0 m) = (30)(9.8)(1.6 m), so F = 118 N ≈ 120 N. A force balance alone cannot decide how the weight is shared between the worker and the ground.

distractorNotes.B: Assumes a uniform pole, with its center of mass at the midpoint, so that F = mg/2.
distractorNotes.C: Uses 2.4 m, the distance from the center of mass to the top end, as the lever arm about the base. That gives the force needed to lift the base end instead.
distractorNotes.D: Sets the worker's force equal to the whole weight, ignoring the ground's upward force on the base end.

items.prompt: A solid rubber ball rolls without slipping down a rough, curved hill. Neglecting air resistance and rolling resistance, is the mechanical energy of the ball–Earth system conserved as the ball rolls down?
choices: No; friction acts on the ball, so it does negative work and converts mechanical energy to internal energy.
Yes; the friction force is perpendicular to the ball's velocity, so it does no work.
No; friction converts translational kinetic energy into rotational kinetic energy, which is not mechanical energy.
Yes; static friction acts at the contact point, which is momentarily at rest, so it does no work.
items.rationale: When a ball rolls without slipping, the point touching the ground is momentarily at rest, so the friction there is static and acts through no displacement: it does no work and dissipates no energy. Gravitational potential energy becomes translational plus rotational kinetic energy, both mechanical, so K_trans + K_rot + U_g stays constant.

distractorNotes.A: That describes kinetic friction during slipping. Without slipping, the contact point does not slide, so the friction is static and does no work.
distractorNotes.B: Friction acts along the hill's surface, parallel to the motion of the ball's center. It does no work because its point of application does not move, not because it is perpendicular to the velocity.
distractorNotes.C: Rotational kinetic energy is mechanical energy. Friction's torque shifts energy between the translational and rotational forms, but K_trans + K_rot + U_g stays constant.

items.prompt: A student sits at rest on a stool that turns without friction about a vertical axis. She holds a bicycle wheel spinning about a vertical axle, with angular momentum L pointing straight up. She then turns the wheel over so that its angular momentum points straight down. Afterward, what is the angular momentum of the student and stool, not counting the wheel?
items.rationale: No external torque acts about the vertical axis, so the total vertical angular momentum of the student, stool and wheel stays L upward. The wheel ends with L downward, so the student and stool must have 2L upward: 2L + (−L) = L.

distractorNotes.B: Gives the student and stool the wheel's change in angular momentum (2L downward) instead of the opposite of that change. The total must stay L upward.
distractorNotes.C: Matches only the wheel's original angular momentum. The student and stool must supply the original L and also cancel the wheel's new L downward.
distractorNotes.D: Treats flipping the wheel as an internal action that changes nothing outside it. The total is unchanged, but her hands exert torques on the wheel, and the wheel exerts opposite torques on her.

items.prompt: A pendulum swings with an amplitude of 4.0°. It is stopped and then released from rest at 8.0°, which is still a small angle. Compared with the original motion, how do the period and the bob's maximum speed change?
choices: The period is unchanged, and the maximum speed doubles.
The period is unchanged, and the maximum speed is multiplied by √2.
The period doubles, and the maximum speed is unchanged.
The period is multiplied by √2, and the maximum speed doubles.
items.rationale: For small amplitudes, T = 2π√(L/g) does not depend on the amplitude, so the period is unchanged. The maximum speed comes from energy: (1/2)v_max^2 = gL(1 − cos θ_0), and for small angles 1 − cos θ_0 ≈ θ_0^2/2, so v_max ≈ θ_0√(gL), in proportion to the amplitude. Doubling the amplitude doubles v_max; the release height becomes four times as great.

distractorNotes.B: Assumes the release height doubles with the angle. The height L(1 − cos θ_0) grows as the square of a small angle, so it quadruples, and v_max = √(2gh) doubles.
distractorNotes.C: A pendulum's small-amplitude period does not depend on the amplitude: the larger swing covers more distance at proportionally greater speed.
distractorNotes.D: The small-angle period depends only on L and g, so it does not change.

items.prompt: A 0.50 kg cart on a level, frictionless track is attached to a horizontal spring with spring constant 20 N/m. The cart is pulled 0.10 m from equilibrium and released from rest. How long does it take to first reach the equilibrium position?
items.rationale: The cart moves in simple harmonic motion with period T = 2π√(m/k) = 2π√(0.50/20) = 0.99 s. Going from maximum displacement to equilibrium is a quarter of a cycle, so t = T/4 ≈ 0.25 s, whatever the amplitude.

distractorNotes.A: Treats the acceleration as constant at its initial value, kA/m = 4.0 m/s^2, and uses x = (1/2)at^2. The spring force shrinks as the cart nears equilibrium, so the cart takes longer than this.
distractorNotes.C: This is half a period, the time to reach the opposite turning point.
distractorNotes.D: This is the full period, the time to return to the release point.

items.prompt: Water flows steadily through a horizontal pipe that narrows from a wide section to a narrow section whose diameter is half as large. The pressure in the wide section is 7.5 kPa greater than in the narrow section. What is the water's speed in the wide section?
items.rationale: Two relations are needed. Continuity: area scales as diameter squared, so A_1 = 4A_2 and v_2 = 4v_1. Bernoulli's equation at equal heights: P_1 − P_2 = (1/2)ρ(v_2^2 − v_1^2) = (1/2)ρ(15v_1^2). So 7500 Pa = (1/2)(1000 kg/m^3)(15)v_1^2, v_1^2 = 1.0 m^2/s^2 and v_1 = 1.0 m/s (and v_2 = 4.0 m/s).

distractorNotes.A: Treats the water in the wide section as at rest, so that (1/2)ρv^2 = ΔP. The water in the wide section moves too, and continuity links the two speeds.
distractorNotes.B: Uses the diameter ratio as the area ratio, v_2 = 2v_1. Area depends on the square of the diameter, so v_2 = 4v_1.
distractorNotes.D: Leaves out the 1/2 in Bernoulli's equation, writing ΔP = ρ(v_2^2 − v_1^2).
